title: Covering the eyes
hookLine: hands circle the candle flames, then cover the eyes while the blessing is said

lines: A LITTLE LONGER THAN THE BLESSING.
cards: Most people have a place to get ten seconds alone. The car in the driveway, engine off. The stairwell at work.

You put your face in your hands, and for a moment nobody needs anything from you. In many Jewish homes, those ten seconds come at the same time every week. Friday, just before sunset, the candles are lit.

The hands circle the flames, then come up over the eyes, and the person lighting stands in the dark of their own palms while the blessing is said. Often they stay there a little longer than the blessing takes.

teach.h: ON DAY TWO: LIGHT, COVER, BLESS.
teach.b: On day two you met the two flames, and the reason for the hands: once the blessing is said, Shabbat has begun, so people light first, cover their eyes, bless, and then look.

teach.h: THE HANDS STAY UP A LITTLE LONGER.
teach.b: Today, stay behind the hands a little longer. The blessing is short: it thanks God, who commanded the lighting of the Sabbath lamp. But in many homes the hands don't come down right away.
People speak quietly, in their own words. For centuries this was one of the few moments in the week that belonged to the woman of the house, and people wrote prayers for it.

teach.h: TKHINES: PRAYERS IN THE KITCHEN'S LANGUAGE.
teach.b: From the sixteen hundreds on, Jewish women in central and eastern Europe used small books of personal prayers in Yiddish, called tkhines.

Many include one for the candles: for a husband's livelihood, for a sick parent, for children who would grow up to love learning. Not the language of the official prayer book: the language of the kitchen.
And the rabbis took their model of personal prayer from a woman. In the first book of Samuel, Hannah, longing for a child, prays at the sanctuary in Shiloh.
In the Jewish Publication Society's 1917 translation: "Now Hannah, she spoke in her heart; only her lips moved, but her voice could not be heard." The priest Eli decides she's drunk.
The Talmud reads the scene the other way: this is how to pray.
The heart turned toward the words, the lips moving, the voice kept low. Watch someone at the candles and you'll often see exactly that. Then the hands come down, and the week is over.

how: Shabbat candles are lit shortly before sunset on Friday; the person lighting often circles their hands over the flames, covers their eyes, says the blessing, and many add quiet words of their own before uncovering their eyes to look at the light.

games.q: you're Eli, the priest at Shiloh. a woman is praying, her lips moving, but no sound comes out. what do you decide?
games.why: Eli decides she's drunk. she's Hannah, pouring out her heart, and the Talmud later makes her quiet prayer the model for everyone's.

practice: Light a candle if it's safe, or just picture one, and rest your hands over your eyes for three slow breaths.
On the first, let the week's noise go quiet; on the second, think of someone you'd hold in your heart if you pray, or simply wish well if you don't.
On the third, lower your hands and look at the first thing you see as if it were new.

wordCard.voice: Tkhines, small books of personal prayers in Yiddish that Jewish women wrote, for the candles and more.

orig.note: Hebrew: the lighting of candles. ner shel Shabbat is the Sabbath lamp named in the blessing.

carryVoice: Your line: eyes closed, the week ends. Behind the hands it ends, and then you look up at the light. Day ninety-nine, done.
